H2S hydrogen bonds because H is bonded to S
CH4 hydrogen bonds because it has H
H2O hydrogen bonds because H is bonded to O

questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonding requires H bonded to N, O, or F. H2S and CH4 lack this, and CO2 has no H at all.
questions.hint: H must bond to N, O, or F.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: Rank dispersion strength by size
questions.stem: A historical case ranks He, Ne, and Ar by London dispersion

options.text: He > Ne > Ar due to decreasing size
Ar > Ne > He due to increasing electron count
All three have equal dispersion
Dispersion depends on polarity not size

questions.explanation: More electrons and larger atoms strengthen London dispersion. Ar has the most electrons, so strongest dispersion. Polarity is not the factor here.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: Compare dipole moments of two bonds
questions.stem: A historical case compares H-F and H-I dipole moments

options.text: Both have equal dipole moments
H-I has a larger dipole moment due to longer bond
H-F has a larger dipole moment than H-I
Dipole moment depends only on bond length

questions.explanation: Fluorine's much higher electronegativity makes H-F more polar than H-I despite the shorter bond. Bond length alone does not determine dipole moment.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: Identify ion-dipole in a solution
questions.stem: A historical case asks what attracts Cl- in water

options.text: No interaction occurs between Cl- and water
Cl- forms covalent bonds with water
Cl- repels all water molecules
Water dipoles attract the Cl- ion

questions.explanation: Ion-dipole attraction occurs when an ion attracts the partial charges of polar water molecules. Covalent bonding and repulsion are not the main interaction.

questions.topic: Formal charge and lone pairs in a polyatomic ion
questions.learningObjective: Compute formal charge on oxygen in OH-
questions.stem: A historical case gives OH- with O having 2 lone pairs and 1 bond; formal charge on O
questions.explanation: Formal charge = 6 - (4 + 1) = -1. Using 2 lone pairs as 2 electrons gives 6-(2+1)=3 which is wrong.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: Correct a mislabeled ionic compound
questions.stem: A historical case labels CuO as copper(I) oxide

options.text: CuO is copper(I) oxide as labeled
CuO is copper(II) oxide because O is -2
CuO is copper(III) oxide
CuO is copper(0) oxide

questions.explanation: One oxide ion at -2 requires Cu2+ for neutrality, so CuO is copper(II) oxide. Copper(I) would need Cu2O.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: Apply metallic bonding to conductivity
questions.stem: A historical case asks why copper is malleable

options.text: Ionic bonds break and reform easily
Covalent bonds stretch and bend easily
Delocalized electrons allow atoms to slide past each other
Metal atoms are not bonded at all

questions.explanation: In metallic bonding, delocalized electrons hold cations together while allowing them to slide, giving malleability. Covalent and ionic models do not explain this.

questions.topic: Valence electrons in the delocalized sea
questions.learningObjective: Count sea electrons for magnesium
questions.stem: A historical case gives magnesium with two valence electrons per atom; sea electrons per 3 atoms
questions.explanation: Each magnesium atom contributes two valence electrons, so 3 atoms contribute 6 electrons to the sea. Counting all electrons gives 36 which is wrong.
questions.hint: Two valence electrons per magnesium atom.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why metals conduct heat
questions.stem: A historical case asks why metals conduct heat well

options.text: No charged particles move in metals
Metal ions vibrate and carry heat only
Covalent bonds stretch to transfer heat
Delocalized electrons transfer kinetic energy quickly

questions.explanation: Delocalized electrons move freely and transfer kinetic energy rapidly, giving high thermal conductivity. Ion vibration alone is not the main mechanism.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Boiling points across a dispersion series
questions.learningObjective: Predict boiling point trend
questions.stem: A historical case asks how many carbon atoms a longer alkane has if boiling point rises
questions.explanation: Longer alkanes have stronger London dispersion and higher boiling points. Octane with 8 carbons boils higher than hexane with 6. The value 8 represents the longer chain length.
questions.hint: Longer chain means higher boiling point.
